startup.name: Aikido Technologies
startup.description: Floating offshore platform that carries a 15MW plus wind turbine, battery storage, backup diesel power and 10MW plus of data halls cooled by the ocean, aimed at gigawatt scale AI datacenters. Customers would be AI compute buyers and offshore power buyers. Five person team.

yc_acceptance.basis: Already accepted, so this is a note. A random applicant starts near 1 percent. Energy and AI infrastructure sit close to YC's interest in hard problems, the pitch is specific and the platform is described as proprietary, which would lift odds, while capital intensity and permitting lower them.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly decline because a floating offshore platform needs hundreds of millions of dollars, years of permitting and marine engineering, which does not fit a three month batch or a small seed check. Reviewers would also doubt that a five person team can show traction before Demo Day.

anchors.adjustment_reason: The Industrials cohort has only 11 companies. The company is mature in concept and sits in a hot AI power theme, but hardware and a 12 month window below $500K check size reduce odds, so about 0.75 of the anchor.

Large round with an anchor compute or utility partner. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed stalls if investors see a shipyard business that needs project finance, not venture capital. With five people and no demonstration unit, the proof is a design and simulations, and generalist seed funds may pass. Kitekraft and OutSail show that hardware teams in wind and marine often raise only small rounds or fail on unsolved physics.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the 0.32 B2B anchor at about 0.85 of it, since demonstrations are expensive and the thin sample says little.

bands.rationale: Thin A funding a scale demonstrator. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.
Typical A for energy hardware with a pilot and offtake letters. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.
Upside if hyperscaler interest in offshore power is real. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A fails if the demonstrator is delayed or the offtake letters are non binding. Compute buyers want power on a known date, and floating wind projects face delays, rising costs and subsidy changes. Microsoft's underwater Natick project ended despite technical success, which shows how hard the cost case is. Posh and Rewbi pivoted after claims on data center speed.

anchors.adjustment_reason: At 0.85 of the anchor; few hardware companies reach B and capital need is far larger.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B fails if the first commercial platform cannot be financed. Offshore projects need banks and utilities, which want a proven unit and a bankable customer. Without a signed compute buyer, investors will not fund fabrication. The nearest analogs, Kitekraft and OutSail, stayed small or shut down.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the all-cohort anchor at 0.7 of it, justified by capital intensity; infrastructure funding may come as project debt that is not a venture round.

Typical infrastructure scale round. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.
Upside gigawatt project funding. Sized from the YC round size tables and current PitchBook figures.

ladder.why_it_fails: The company stops before a Series C if the first projects are late or uneconomic, because later rounds fund construction, not engineering. A hyperscaler building onshore power faster, or cheaper onshore nuclear and gas, would remove the reason to go offshore. Capital can also arrive as project finance that does not count as an equity round.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely failure is that the economics of offshore datacenters do not beat onshore power, and the platform never gets built at scale. Delays in permitting, marine engineering and financing stretch the timeline beyond seed and Series A runway. If it does exit, the buyer is more likely an offshore wind or shipbuilding firm than a hyperscaler.

analogs.outcome_summary: Began in 2024 with an underwater data center plan that drew regulator scrutiny for lacking permits; no funding was confirmed.

analogs.outcome_summary: Small pre-seed and a $1.6M round after years, a grid connected flight, still small.
Raised pre-seed and seed, then was shut down after fundamental physics problems.

analogs.outcome_summary: Seed of $3.8M in 2022 for another business, pivoted to modular data centers, no later priced round found.

analogs.outcome_summary: Small seed only, then shut down.

killers.risk: Capital intensity and offshore permitting outrun venture runway
killers.evidence: Floating wind faces delays, higher costs and interest rates, and OutSail and Kitekraft struggled to fund marine and wind hardware.
killers.mitigation: Partner with a shipyard and a utility for project finance, and stage the build with a small demonstration.

killers.risk: Offshore economics lose to onshore power and gas for AI datacenters
killers.evidence: Microsoft ended its underwater Natick project after a technical success, and hyperscalers are building onshore at scale.
killers.mitigation: Target regions with grid constraints and sell power plus compute as a package.

killers.risk: No bankable compute customer signs before fabrication
killers.evidence: Rewbi and Posh pivoted after data center claims without confirmed rounds, a sign that buyers are slow to commit to unproven capacity.
killers.mitigation: Secure non binding then binding offtake with a neocloud and show a scale test.

competition_now.name: Microsoft Project Natick
competition_now.what: Underwater data center experiment, ended in 2024 after servers failed less than on land.

competition_now.name: Onshore hyperscale and neocloud builders
competition_now.what: Conventional data centers and power deals that the offshore idea must beat on cost and speed.

technical_complexity.rationale: Marine structures, floating wind turbines, battery integration, cooling and data hall reliability at sea are each hard, and the pitch combines them. A five person team can design but cannot easily build or certify it without partners.

takeover_risk.rationale: Replicating a floating platform plus data halls takes years of engineering and certification, and few large firms have the incentive to move first, so a quick copy is unlikely, though a large wind firm could partner or acquire.

evidence.claim: AI compute demand is power constrained, and operators look for new sites; offshore concepts are explored by several groups, though the concept itself is unproven.

roadmap.goal: Show a credible scale test and a first customer letter.
actions: Build a small scale platform or tank test with a shipyard partner.
Sign a non binding offtake with a compute buyer.
roadmap.proof: Test data and a named buyer letter.

roadmap.goal: Fund a demonstrator and a project site.
actions: Secure site and permit pathway in one jurisdiction.
Line up a project finance partner.
roadmap.proof: Permit application accepted and a funded demonstrator.

pros.evidence: Compute demand is limited by power and sites, so any new power plus compute supply gets attention.

pros.point: Free ocean cooling is real physics
pros.evidence: Natick found fewer server failures than on land.

brand.name: Aikido Technologies
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Aikido Technologies" --era 2022+ : kind name_plus_descriptor, alive 93.7 percent, n=557
strengths: Aikido suggests using the force of the wave
weaknesses: Technologies suffix is generic and tells nothing
brand.rationale: The martial art name hints at working with natural forces and is distinctive, while the Technologies suffix is typical of industrial firms. It will not affect infrastructure buyers who decide on cost and risk.

narrative.headline: A bold, power hungry AI infrastructure bet that probably gets a seed but faces large capital and proof hurdles after that.
narrative.general_summary: Aikido Technologies proposes gigawatt scale floating wind platforms with data halls cooled by the ocean. The need is real, since AI compute is constrained by power, and the pitch connects to a hot theme, which makes a seed above the YC check likely though not certain. The difficulty is that offshore marine hardware is expensive, slow to permit and slow to build, onshore power competes, and the nearest analogs in marine and wind hardware stayed small or failed. Reaching Series A needs a demonstrator and a named buyer, and later rounds depend on project finance, not venture capital. About 60 percent of simulated paths stall or shut down, and the upside is large but rare.

assumptions: Blind forecast as of 2026-10-05 using only the batch description.
Industrials cohort is only 11 companies, so B2B cohorts were also used.
